conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: FailedTickExtensionReversalSignal
candidates.quote: A five- or nine-tick failed breakout is common at the end of a protracted trend and is often the first sign of a reversal.
candidates.description: Near the end of a protracted trend, if price extends only failureTicks beyond a reference extreme (e.g. a signal bar or recent swing extreme) and fails to continue, treat that failed extension as a reversal signal and consider trading the opposite direction one tick beyond the failure bar.
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop one tick below the failure bar (mirrored: buy stop one tick above)

complexity.reason: 'end of a protracted trend' is a design decision (a research-grade always-in/trend-duration concept); the extension-and-failure arithmetic itself is trivial once a reference extreme is chosen

notes: Related to ranges chapter 5's failed-breakout/breakout-pullback primitives (already mined); this is the fixed-tick (5 or 9 ticks), Emini-scalp-specific variant of that idea.

candidates.name: BreakevenStopAfterFixedFavorableMove
candidates.quote: and then to breakeven after a five-tick move, this further reduces the required winning percentage to be profitable on the day.
candidates.description: Once open profit reaches favorableTicks beyond the entry price, move the protective stop to breakeven (the entry price) for the remainder of the position.
candidates.book_order_type: stop order moved to the original entry price

complexity.reason: needs EntryPrice plus a persistent once-true flag tracking whether the favorable-move threshold has ever been reached

notes: Equivalent to ProfitProtector with maxProfit set to the dollar value of favorableTicks and retracement = 0 (exit once profit gives back to breakeven).

candidates.name: StopTightenToEntryBarUnconditional
candidates.quote: If you move your stop from the signal bar extreme to the entry bar extreme (one tick beyond both) after the entry bar closes...
candidates.description: Once the entry bar closes, unconditionally move the stop from the signal-bar extreme to the entry-bar extreme (one tick beyond it), regardless of the entry bar's body strength.
candidates.book_order_type: protective stop moved to one tick beyond the entry bar

complexity.reason: needs BarsSinceEntry to fire exactly once after the entry bar closes and persistent stop-price state

notes: Near-duplicate of ranges chapter 27's TightenStopAfterStrongEntryBar (R27-02), but stated here without the 'strong body' qualifier -- an unconditional tightening rather than a conditional one. The dedup pass should decide whether these are the same rule or two distinct variants.

candidates.name: ScalpProfitTargetEqualsRisk
candidates.quote: In general, the potential reward (the number of ticks to the profit target) is about the size of the risk (the number of ticks to the protective stop).
candidates.description: A scalp's profit target is set at approximately the same distance from entry as its protective stop.
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at a price equidistant from entry as the protective stop

complexity.reason: single arithmetic comparison once the stop distance is known

candidates.name: SwingProfitTargetTwiceRisk
candidates.quote: Intraday swing traders... Their potential reward is usually at least twice as large as their risk.
candidates.description: A swing trade's profit target is set at least twice the distance from entry as its protective stop.
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at least twice the stop distance from entry

complexity.reason: single arithmetic comparison once the stop distance is known

notes: Same shape as R24-04 with a different ratio; kept as a separate candidate since Brooks explicitly distinguishes the scalp (1:1) and swing (2:1 or better) styles as different rules.

candidates.name: MinimumDailyVolumeFilter
candidates.quote: It is relatively easy to look for swings in high-volume stocks (at least three million shares per day, but preferably seven million or more)...
candidates.description: Only take swing setups in a symbol whose (daily) bar volume exceeds a minimum threshold.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (symbol/context filter, not an order placement)
notes: Unlike VolumeAboveAverageMultiple (relative to the symbol's own rolling average), this is an absolute share-count threshold intended for daily bars/symbol selection.

candidates.name: AddOnReentryAfterStopRunContinuation
candidates.quote: if it comes back and runs those stops and then immediately resumes the new trend, reenter or add to your swing position at one tick beyond the prior bar (in a new bull trend, this is one tick above the prior bar's high).
candidates.description: After price briefly trades beyond a recent breakeven-stop cluster (i.e., beyond a recent swing extreme or entry level) against the trade direction, but then immediately closes back in the trend direction, add to (or re-enter) the position on a stop one tick beyond the prior bar's extreme.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the prior bar's high

complexity.reason: needs to track a recent stop-cluster/swing-extreme level and detect a brief breach-and-reclaim before applying the ordinary breakout-stop mechanization

notes: Likely overlaps with the failed-breakout/breakout-pullback family already mined in ranges chapter 5.

candidates.name: FilledAtExtremeMoreTrendPressureReentry
candidates.quote: If the market touches the profit target limit order but does not go through it and the order is still filled, that means that there might be more trend pressure than is evident on the chart... Look for opportunities to get long again.
candidates.description: When a profit-taking limit exit is filled at exactly the extreme tick of a move (the market did not need to trade through the price to fill it), treat this as a sign of unusual trend strength and look to re-enter in the original direction.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (a fill-quality observation used as a re-entry filter)

complexity.reason: depends on modeling a subtle broker-fill distinction (touched-and-filled vs. traded-through) that most backtest fill models do not expose the same way real limit orders behave

candidates.name: ScaleOutPartialPositionAtRewardMultiple
candidates.quote: exit 25 to 75 percent of your contracts at a scalper's profit that is equal to at least one to two times your initial risk, and then scale out of the remaining contracts as the market continues to go your way.
candidates.description: Exit a fraction of the position once open profit reaches a multiple of the initial risk, then move the stop on the remainder to around breakeven and scale out further as the trade continues.
candidates.book_order_type: limit order on part of the position, remainder trailed

complexity.reason: requires the strategy engine to support partial-position exits with independent stop management on the remainder, which is a design decision beyond a single boolean exit condition

rejected.quote: An investor is someone who buys stocks based on fundamentals and plans to hold the stocks for six months to many years, allowing time for the beneficial fundamentals to be reflected in the price of the stock.
rejected.reason: defines a trading style by fundamentals and holding intent, not a bar-level test

rejected.quote: A common cause of losses is putting on a trade, watching it become a loser, not exiting at your planned stop, and instead convincing yourself that it is fine to convert the trade into an investment.
rejected.reason: pure psychology/discipline discussion, no bar-level condition proposed

rejected.quote: If you are confident, one guideline is to assume that you believe that the chance of success is at least 60 percent.
rejected.reason: a subjective probability estimate the trader forms, not something computed from bars

rejected.quote: Instead of worrying about taking 20 trades a day and trying to make one point on each, what about just scalping the very best three trades of the day...
rejected.reason: pure discretion about which setups to cherry-pick, no bar-level test proposed

rejected.quote: Incidentally, I had a friend many years ago who used to trade 100 Emini contracts at a time, scalping two ticks on about 25 trades a day. Since he lived in a 12,000-square-foot house, I assume that he was doing well.

Although all stocks trade basically the same way, there are subtle personality differences between them. For example, Apple (AAPL) is very respectful when it comes to testing breakouts, whereas Goldman Sachs (GS) tends to run stops, requiring a wider stop.
rejected.reason: anecdotal per-symbol characterization with no defined bar-level test

chapter_summary: Mostly a conceptual/statistical discussion distinguishing investors, traders, scalpers, and swing traders and the trader's-equation probability math behind each style; the bulk of the chapter (and its two worked-example figures, which just re-illustrate high2/high3/high4, double top/bottom, wedge, and two-bar-reversal patterns already mined elsewhere) is not mechanizable and is reflected in a larger-than-usual rejected list. The genuinely new candidates are: a fixed-tick failed-extension reversal signal (5/9 ticks, common late in a trend), two stop-management rules (breakeven ratchet after a fixed favorable move; unconditional tightening to the entry bar, a near-duplicate of chapter 27's conditional version), two reward:risk profit-target exits (1:1 for scalps, 2:1 for swings, both likely duplicates of the existing TakeProfitWithRatioStop rule), an absolute daily-volume symbol filter, a stop-run-then-continuation add-on entry, a research-grade limit-fill-quality re-entry signal, and a partial-position scale-out exit framework that the engine may not support as a single boolean condition.
